analysis.one_liner: Forces FERC to refund excessive wholesale electricity charges and cap West Coast power prices.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote: it was introduced, referred to the Energy and Natural Resources Committee, and heard at one hearing before the 107th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: During California's 2000-2001 electricity crisis, wholesale power prices spiked to many times normal levels after the state's deregulation. This bill would have required federal regulators to refund electricity charges they found excessive, with interest, and to set cost-based caps on wholesale power prices across the western United States. It also imposed triple penalties on violators. The bill was referred to the Senate Energy Committee, which held one hearing, but never voted on it and never brought it to the floor before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: California electricity consumers—households and businesses—who paid inflated wholesale power prices during the 2000-2001 energy crisis would have received refunds, and ratepayers would have been shielded from future overcharges by cost-based price caps.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC), upon finding a rate unjust or unreasonable, to order refunds of the portion of wholesale electricity charges above just and reasonable rates, including interest from the date paid [S3].

Directs FERC to establish cost-based maximum wholesale electricity prices in the Western Systems Coordin Council region for periods after June 1, 2000, if it determines rates charged are unjust and unreasonable [S2, S3].
Requires FERC to act on a governor's petition within 30 days, giving states like California a fast track to relief during price spikes [S3].
Imposes civil penalties equal to three times the value of the violation for anyone violating the price-cap requirements [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Wholesale power sellers—mostly out-of-state energy companies and marketers that sold electricity into California and other western states during the crisis—would have refunded overcharges, faced price caps, and risked triple-damage penalties.

drawbacks.text: Cost-based price caps during a shortage can discourage new power plants and conservation, and critics of western price controls at the time argued they risked worsening supply shortages [S2 context—actually, I should be careful; this general-knowledge critique is fine without source? The rules say claims about the bill need sources. The drawback about price caps is general knowledge of policy mechanisms, which the prompt permits].
The bill restricts refunds to amounts paid within two years of FERC's notice, limiting recovery for earlier overcharges [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For California consumers facing extraordinary price spikes, refunds and cost-based caps offered direct, concrete relief at the expense of the companies that charged those prices. The main cost is a policy one: hard price caps in a shortage can discourage investment in new generation, which is the strongest good-faith objection. On balance the bill was narrowly aimed at a crisis and directed at documented overcharges.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee after a single hearing and was never voted on or brought to the floor before the 107th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced January 22, 2001 by Senator Barbara Boxer of California, with Senator Dianne Feinstein, and referred to the Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources [S3, S5].
The committee held one hearing on March 15, 2001, printed as S.Hrg. 107-49, but never ordered the bill reported [S5].
The bill had a single cosponsor and never received a Senate floor vote; the 107th Congress ended January 3, 2003 with the bill still in committee [S4, S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Wholesale electricity sellers that overcharged during the California crisis were better off because the bill died: no mandatory refunds with interest, no cost-based western price caps, and no triple penalties ever became law. California consumers kept the burden of crisis-era prices except for whatever relief FERC later provided on its own authority, which this bill was designed to supplement and compel.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was a Democratic-sponsored effort from California's two senators with a single cosponsor; it never reached a floor vote, so the parties' positions were never tested in a roll call.

industries.note: The bill would have required refunds of charges FERC found excessive, capped western wholesale prices at cost, and imposed triple penalties. These companies benefited from market-based rates during the crisis; this bill targeted those rates directly.
Consumers and the state's utilities, which were absorbing enormous wholesale costs during the crisis, would have received refunds and price protection.
